subtype: Screaming and shrieking in play or upset [Expressing]
passage: At the park by their apartment block, Tarun, two, shrieked with delight as Nilesh pushed the swing higher, his arms flung wide, eyes bright. When it slowed and stopped, he screamed just as loud but with a different sound, sharp and cross, his face crumpled. “Again!” Later a large dog lunged out of the gate, and Tarun let out a high scream, froze and grabbed Nilesh's leg. Nilesh scooped him up, checking the dog was on the lead. “Loud dog. I've got you.”

qa.q: What did Tarun do when the swing stopped?
qa.a: He screamed loudly in a cross, sharp way and shouted “Again!”

qa.q: How could Nilesh tell that Tarun's screams meant different things?
qa.a: Nilesh looked at the face and the setting: bright eyes on the swing meant joy, the crumpled face after the stop meant annoyance, and freezing at the dog meant fear. Nilesh could still be wrong, so kept checking.

qa.q: What could Nilesh do after the dog scare?
qa.a: Nilesh could hold Tarun until he calms and let him look at dogs from a distance in future.

qa.q: How might other parents in the park feel?
qa.a: They may be startled by the screams, but Nilesh's calm response would show it is a normal part of toddler life.

grounding: A toddler shrieks in delight, frustration and fear, and the same loud sound is read through the face, the setting and what just happened.

subtype: Screaming and shrieking in play or upset [Expressing]
passage:
“Rafiq, you're splashing!” said Jahnavi.
Rafiq shrieked with laughter and slapped the water again, sending spray over the mirror.
“That's a happy squeal.”
“More!”
Later at the gate, a big dog barked and Rafiq gave a high, sharp scream and hid behind her.
“That's a scared scream. I know.” She picked him up.
At dinner, Jahnavi took his cup away and he screamed a third kind, low and angry.
“And that one is cross.”

qa.q: Where was Rafiq when he squealed with laughter?
qa.a: In the bath, splashing water.

qa.q: How does Jahnavi work out what each of Rafiq's screams means?
qa.a: She uses the setting and what just happened: joy at splashing, fear at the dog and anger at losing his cup. She might sometimes need more clues.

qa.q: What could Jahnavi do to help him with the dog?
qa.a: She could keep him close, stay calm and let him watch dogs from a distance.

qa.q: How might Rafiq feel when Jahnavi names the sound?
qa.a: He may feel understood and slowly learn words for his feelings. 🙂

grounding: A toddler shrieks in delight, fear and anger, and the caregiver reads the sound with the setting and what just happened.

subtype: Screaming and shrieking in play or upset [Expressing]
passage: Playgroup note, Thursday. Tarun screamed twice this morning, and they were very different. On the swing, he screamed at the top of the arc, face bright and eyes shining, and asked for "more!" Later, in the sandpit, his shoe came off, and he screamed again with a red, scrunched face, stamping his foot. I pushed the swing higher the first time and helped with the shoe the second. Dhruv, playgroup teacher

qa.q: What came off in the sandpit?
qa.a: Tarun's shoe.

qa.q: How did Dhruv tell what each of Tarun's screams meant?
qa.a: By reading his face and the setting: a bright face on the swing meant joy and excitement, while a red, scrunched face and stamping in the sandpit meant frustration.

qa.q: What would you advise a new helper about Tarun's screams?
qa.a: Look at his face and at what just happened before reacting, since the same scream can mean joy or frustration.

qa.q: How might Tarun's parents feel reading this note?
qa.a: They would likely feel reassured that Dhruv understands Tarun's loud sounds and responds to each one properly.

grounding: A teacher reads a toddler's screams by face and setting, finding one joyful and one frustrated.

subtype: Screaming and shrieking in play or upset [Expressing]
passage:
At the edge of the village pond, a duck waddled right up to Suraj and quacked. Suraj let out a piercing shriek.
Rafiq, the older boy from next door, jumped forward to pull him back. Then he saw Suraj's face: mouth wide, eyes crinkled, both hands clapping.
Rafiq laughed and crouched beside him. "You like it!" Suraj shrieked again, bouncing, as the duck quacked back.

qa.q: What did the duck do to Suraj?
qa.a: It waddled right up to him and quacked.

qa.q: What was Suraj feeling when he shrieked?
qa.a: He was excited and delighted, not scared, as his crinkled eyes and clapping hands showed.

qa.q: What did Rafiq do that helped him read the shriek correctly?
qa.a: He looked at Suraj's face and hands before pulling him away, instead of reacting to the sound alone.

qa.q: What would change if Rafiq had pulled Suraj away without looking?
qa.a: Suraj would have lost a happy moment and might have become upset at being dragged off.

grounding: An older boy reads a toddler's shriek by his face and finds joy, not fear.

subtype: Screaming and shrieking in play or upset [Expressing]
passage:
On the playground in Buenos Aires, Santiago pushed his little brother Rafael higher and higher on the swing. Rafael screamed.
"You love it, right?" Santiago pushed again.
Another scream. This time Santiago looked properly. Rafael's face was scrunched, his knuckles white on the chains, and he wasn't looking at the sky but down at the ground.
Santiago caught the swing and slowed it. "Too high. Sorry." Rafael's scream turned into a shaky breath.

qa.q: Where was Rafael looking when Santiago looked properly?
qa.a: Down at the ground, not at the sky.

qa.q: What was Rafael feeling when he screamed the second time?
qa.a: He was frightened by how high the swing was going, as his scrunched face and white knuckles showed.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Santiago assumed the scream meant fun; looking at Rafael's face and grip showed fear, and slowing the swing fixed it.

qa.q: How might Santiago feel after slowing the swing?
qa.a: He may feel sorry for pushing too high and glad he noticed in time.

grounding: A brother learns to read his toddler brother's scream by face and grip, and finds fear rather than joy.

subtype: Screaming and shrieking in play or upset [Expressing]
passage:
I'm Ritu. My little sister Payal shrieks a lot, and it took me ages to work out that her shrieks aren't all the same.
At the splash pool on Sunday she shrieked every time the water hit her, and she was grinning and kicking.
Ten minutes later our cousin grabbed her bucket. Same shriek, but her face went red and her fists shook.
Mummy didn't just hear the noise. She looked at Payal's face and at the bucket, then said, “You're cross! He took it."

qa.q: Where did Payal shriek every time the water hit her?
qa.a: At the splash pool on Sunday.

qa.q: What was Payal feeling with each shriek?
qa.a: At the splash pool she was delighted, shown by her grin and kicking; when her bucket was taken she was angry, shown by her red face and shaking fists.

qa.q: How did Mummy work out what Payal's shriek meant?
qa.a: She looked at Payal's face and what had just happened with the bucket, instead of judging by the sound alone.

qa.q: What was confusing for Ritu about Payal's shrieks?
qa.a: The sound was the same whether Payal was happy or cross, so Ritu had to watch her face and the situation to tell.

grounding: It shows a toddler shrieking in delight and screaming in frustration, with a caregiver reading her face and the setting to tell which.
